summary: Describes PASTE, an architecture that lets internet service providers combine differentiated services with traffic engineering. It is a design proposal for provider networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a plan for how a company that runs a big network can send some traffic by faster roads and manage where all the cars go.

questions: how can isps combine diffserv and traffic engineering
how can isps provide differentiated services scalably
how do explicit routes work in paste
subtitle: How ISPs can combine traffic engineering with differentiated services using MPLS and RSVP.

tldr.problem: ISPs want to offer different service levels (priority vs. best-effort) and control where traffic flows to avoid congestion. But tracking individual flows would require too much state. ISPs need a scalable way to bundle flows into managed trunks.
tldr.mechanism: PASTE uses MPLS to create labeled tunnels (traffic trunks) that carry aggregated flows of the same traffic class along explicit paths. RSVP sets up these trunks and reserves bandwidth. Traffic classes are encoded in MPLS labels or IPv4 ToS fields.
tldr.outcome: ISPs can offer priority services with guaranteed quality, route traffic away from congestion, and support service level agreements with each other, while keeping the state requirements manageable as the network grows.

facts.label: Routing control
facts.value: Explicit Route Object (ERO) with strict/loose hops

today: RFC 2430 is an informational document describing the PASTE architecture. While PASTE as specified was not widely adopted, its core ideas—aggregating flows into trunks, combining traffic engineering with QoS, and using MPLS to enable explicit routing—became foundational to modern ISP network design. MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE) and Segment Routing have evolved these concepts.

sections.title: The Challenge of Differentiated Services at Scale
sections.content:
Internet service providers want to offer differentiated services: some traffic gets priority (lower latency, guaranteed bandwidth), while most traffic gets best-effort delivery. They also want to do traffic engineering: direct traffic away from congested links toward uncongested routes, making more efficient use of their network.

The challenge is scalability. If an ISP tries to maintain separate state for each flow (each TCP connection, each UDP stream), the amount of state grows with the number of flows, which grows with the size of the internet. This violates fundamental scalability principles.

PASTE solves this by aggregating flows of the same traffic class into traffic trunks, which are MPLS tunnels. A single trunk carries many flows, so the state an ISP must maintain grows with the number of trunks, not the number of flows. For example, an ISP might have one priority trunk to each destination instead of thousands of priority flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of marking each package individually, the ISP sorts packages into priority and regular mail, then moves each pile as a unit. This way the ISP only has to track a few piles instead of millions of packages.

sections.title: Traffic Trunks and Traffic Classes
sections.content:
PASTE defines three traffic classes. Best Effort traffic has no guarantees and makes up most of today's internet traffic (web browsing, email, file downloads). Priority traffic has explicit resource reservations and may require bandwidth guarantees, jitter bounds, or delay limits (VoIP, video, mission-critical data). Network Control traffic consists of routing protocols and network management, which must be preserved even under congestion.

A traffic trunk (or simply trunk) is a single MPLS tunnel that carries aggregated flows of a single traffic class along a single path. The trunk has a specific ingress router, egress router, and explicit path. All flows in a trunk share the same resources and are forwarded by the same label-switching operations.

The number of trunks in an ISP network is bounded. In the worst case with N routers and C traffic classes, there could be N * (N-1) * C trunks. But in practice, trunks can be merged when they share the same path, reducing the actual number. The key insight is that the number of trunks is independent of the number of flows, enabling the architecture to scale.
sections.plainLanguage: A trunk is a convoy of trucks carrying the same type of cargo (priority mail, regular mail, or control messages). All trucks in a convoy travel the same route and stop at the same places.

sections.title: MPLS, RSVP, and Explicit Routing
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) wraps packets in a minimal header containing a label. Each label identifies a path and a set of forwarding rules. Label-switching routers forward packets based on labels, not IP addresses, enabling fast switching and explicit path control.

RSVP, the Resource Reservation Protocol, is used to set up trunks and reserve bandwidth. When a router needs to establish a trunk, it sends RSVP messages to reserve resources along a path. RSVP is extended with an Explicit Route Object (ERO) that specifies the exact sequence of routers the trunk must traverse. A router can list some hops as "strict" (no other routers in between) or "loose" (other routers allowed), giving the ISP fine-grained control over paths.

RSVP in PASTE differs from its original use: instead of reserving resources for individual flows from host to host, RSVP reserves resources for trunks from router to router. The path is determined by the ISP's explicit route, not by destination-based routing. This allows traffic engineering: the ISP can steer traffic around known congestion points.

Traffic classes are encoded in the MPLS label (in 3 CoS bits) or in the IPv4 ToS byte (3 precedence bits). As a packet travels through a trunk, its traffic class is preserved in the label, allowing intermediate routers to apply different queuing or drop policies based on class.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is like a stamp on the package that says 'forward to door 5'. RSVP is the reservation system that says 'I need door 5 to be available'. The explicit route is the list of doors the package goes through.

sections.title: The PASTE Architecture
sections.content:
PASTE combines five functional components into a coordinated architecture:

Traffic classes divide packets into Best Effort, Priority, and Network Control groups. Trunks bundle flows of the same class into a single MPLS tunnel with explicit routing. RSVP establishes trunks, reserves bandwidth, and updates traffic control state. Traffic engineering uses explicit routes to direct trunks away from congestion. Traffic shaping and policing at ISP boundaries ensure that trunks comply with service level agreements: the sender shapes outbound traffic to match the agreed profile, and the receiver polices incoming traffic to reject traffic that exceeds the profile.

Inter-Provider SLAs (IPSs) are bilateral agreements between ISPs about how to handle trunks that cross ISP boundaries. An IPS specifies which traffic classes can be exchanged, how much volume each ISP will accept, and what compensation (if any) will be paid. Multilateral IPSs involve more than two ISPs.

An ISP may also establish backup trunks for reliability. If the primary trunk fails, the backup trunk can be activated. The status of the primary trunk is monitored via out-of-band mechanisms such as the Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP).
sections.plainLanguage: The architecture is like a postal system: sort mail into classes, put each class into a truck (trunk), reserve capacity for each truck along a specific route, make sure each truck does not exceed its cargo limit, and make agreements with other postal services about sharing trucks.

sections.title: Example: A Voice Call Across Multiple ISPs
sections.content:
Consider a Voice over IP call from user S to user D. The call data packets are priority traffic (low jitter, low drop). Suppose S is in ISP F, and D is in ISP L, with the traffic passing through ISPs X, Y, and Z.

Step 1: RSVP propagation. S generates an RSVP PATH message describing the call (3 kbps, low jitter, low latency). The message propagates through ISP F's network to exit router E. Router E has a trunk connecting ISPs F → X → Z → L and determines that the call's requirements fit the trunk. Router E encapsulates the PATH message inside the trunk and sends it across the ISP boundary, where router U decapsulates it and propagates it to D.

Step 2: Data propagation. Voice packets from S flow through ISP F to router E, where they are given an MPLS label and inserted into the trunk. Label-switching routers forward the packet using the label (not IP lookup). At intermediate routers, the traffic class is preserved in the CoS bits. The packet may be aggregated into another trunk crossing the next ISP boundary, and finally decapsulates in ISP L at router U, then flows to D.

Step 3: Trunk management. The primary trunk from ISP F through X and Z to L may be established via a multilateral agreement. The path uses strict hops at ISP boundaries and loose hops in between, giving each ISP flexibility within its own network. Backup trunks provide redundancy. If the primary trunk fails, a backup trunk can be activated without losing the call.
sections.plainLanguage: A voice call enters ISP F as a regular voice stream, gets a special label at the ISP boundary, travels through ISP X and Z with that label, gets relabeled at each boundary, and arrives at ISP L as a regular voice stream again.
